label: Money & maths tip
items: Round-number trick: 10% is a moved decimal point, 20% is double it, 15% is 10% plus half of it.
An extra payment on a loan early in the term saves the most interest.
Rule of 72: divide 72 by your annual return to estimate years to double.
Bi-weekly mortgage payments (26 half-payments) make one extra full payment a year.
A 50% rise followed by a 50% fall leaves you 25% down.
Two discounts of 20% and 10% make 28% off, not 30%.
Compare loans by the total cost, not just the monthly payment.
Starting to save five years earlier can matter more than saving more later.
Check the sales-tax rate before a big purchase; it changes the real price.
To remove tax from a total, divide by 1 plus the tax rate, not subtract the percentage.
A salary divided by 2,080 gives a rough hourly rate for a full-time job.
Fuel cost per trip: distance times litres per 100 km, divided by 100, times the price.
BMI is a rough screening number. It cannot tell muscle from fat.
Percentage points and percent are different: 3% to 4% is +1 point but +33%.
A margin of error of 3 points means a 48-46 poll lead is within the noise.
Round the tip up to a whole share when paying cash; it keeps splitting simple.
Use the median, not the average, when a few big numbers pull things up.
Savings goal? Divide the target by the months left to get the monthly amount.
Interest on a loan front-loads: early payments are mostly interest.
Check your result with a rough estimate first; if they disagree, look for a typo.
The higher the interest rate, the more valuable each extra payment is.
Unit conversions: 1 inch is exactly 2.54 cm; 1 mile is 1.609344 km.
Use a longer time horizon when comparing investments; one year tells you very little.
Fees of 1-2% a year can quietly take a third of long-term growth.
Know your hourly value: it helps you decide what to outsource.
To compare unit prices, divide price by quantity at every size.
Dates: add 7 days for a week, but months have different lengths, so check.
Inflation of 3% halves buying power in about 24 years (rule of 72).
An emergency fund of three to six months of expenses protects against surprises.
Always sanity-check currency amounts for the right number of zeros.
